svg.text: Cache flush — broadcast write to the last core's completion read

One flush primitive exists: whole-cache invalidate-and-writeback, requested by a flush token (a MemReq with attr.is_flush). Every ordered path carries its own token, and a cache answers a token only after flushing the next level.

flush_ready gates the counter, so the walk pauses whenever the memory-request queue is near full.
A write-through bank never gates on it — it emits no writebacks at all.

Why one token per memory port
Each port is a separately buffered path to the next level, and nothing orders one port's
writes against another port's token. A single token could reach the next level while another
port's last writes are still queued in front of it: that level's walk would release the token
and the writes would land after the walk, still dirty. A token behind each port's own data
is answered only once that data is in. The same rule gives one token per dcache lane.
The no-ack equivalent of waiting for store acknowledgements on every path.
Why done is level-held rather than a pulse
One core's flush fans out to every dcache lane, the icache, and — with graphics enabled — the
socket and cluster gfx caches. Each leg finishes at a different time. Holding every
done high until req drops lets the parent simply AND them together, race-free.
A pulse would need a latch at every junction and would drop legs that finished early.
What the block buys
While any token is visible, no core request can reach any bank pipeline. That is what lets
STATE_FLUSH assume the only in-flight entries are its own walk, makes every memory response
in STATE_FORWARD a token response, and makes a late token safe: it can only become visible
once all of its input's earlier requests were accepted, before the walk.
The cost: the cache is effectively OFF for the walk. Flush is linear in cache size.
Walk length
write-through: LINES_PER_BANK
write-back: LINES_PER_BANK x NUM_WAYS
Write-through clears all ways in parallel (no way_en gate), so one pass over the lines
suffices. Write-back must visit each (way, line) separately because each dirty line
emits its own memory request. All banks walk concurrently.
Reset reuses the same machinery
The FSM's reset state is STATE_INIT, not STATE_IDLE: it walks every line clearing valid
bits, so the tag SRAM needs no async reset — which is what makes it map cleanly to BRAM.
A flush arriving during init is latched and answered immediately: init already invalidated
everything, so the init walk stands in for the flush walk.
